title: Evans Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Evans wells have a 49 ft median depth, but finished well costs commonly run $8,400-$15,400.
h1: What Evans, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Evans means looking beyond the fact that a property has a well permit. Local records show shallow wells are common, but the construction record is uneven: 2,669 permits are on file, while 1,605 wells are recorded as constructed and 1,591 report a total depth.

Within 5 miles of Evans, the typical completed well is much shallower than many Colorado mountain or foothill wells. Even so, a permit record does not guarantee usable water, safe water, or enough water for a proposed home. Neighboring well construction, static water levels, intended use, and the actual site geology all matter.

sections.heading: Evans wells are usually shallow, but the range is wide
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Evans is 49 feet. The middle half runs from 27 to 75 feet, and 90% of reported wells are under 100 feet. That pattern gives a driller a useful starting point for a bid, but it is not a promise for a particular lot.

The records also include wells reaching 900 feet. About 9% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and a smaller share is deeper. Evans sits on Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, with permits commonly naming Denver Basin aquifer units. Local alluvial deposits and the exact location of water-bearing material can change the design, casing, grout, and final depth.

sections.heading: Reported Evans yields are generally strong
sections.html:
Among the 265 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is listed from 15.0 to 900.0 gallons per minute, and 82% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 3% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, while none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures are encouraging for ordinary household planning, but the sample is much smaller than the total permit history. A reported yield is not the same as guaranteed long-term production. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, permitted use, and any limits tied to the permit. An exempt household-use well is still subject to Colorado rules, including the 35 gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Evans water levels do not show a simple steady decline
sections.html:
The median static water level is 13 feet below the ground surface. The middle half of reported measurements is 8 to 19 feet, so many wells encounter water relatively close to the surface. That can reduce drilling depth, but shallow groundwater also deserves careful testing because it can be more exposed to nearby land uses.

The decade series does not show a straight downward trend. The median was 20 feet below surface in the 1960s, 9 feet in the 2010s, and 13 feet in the 2020s. Measurements come from different wells and locations, so treat this as local historical context rather than a prediction for a vacant parcel.

sections.heading: Permit activity continues around Evans
sections.html:
Evans has a long well-permit history, with permits issued from the 1950s through the 2020s. The newest permit in the records is from 2025. The 2020s account for 399 permits, compared with 357 in the 1990s, so recent activity is substantial.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Clement, Glenn A., and Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed). Those names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a driller serves a particular property today. For a purchase, compare nearby construction reports rather than relying only on the driller name.

sections.heading: A typical Evans well costs more than the hole itself
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 49-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,400 to $3,400. That is only the drilling portion.

A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $8,400 to $15,400. A shallow well can still require substantial site work, access, casing, grout, pump equipment, and utility connections. Get a written bid that identifies what is included and what happens if the driller must go deeper or the hole does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic room, and low-yield risk
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 2,478 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove a specific Evans well is contaminated, but it is enough reason to test before closing and to review the well location relative to nearby land uses. A qualified laboratory can identify the appropriate drinking-water panel.

Low yield and dry holes are still possible even though recorded yields are favorable. Before building, confirm the permitted use, well location, setbacks, septic area, driveway access, and available electrical service. Shallow water also makes careful septic design and maintenance important. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement may affect what use is allowed.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Evans, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Evans is 49 feet. The middle half runs from 27 to 75 feet, and 90% are under 100 feet. The record is not uniform, however: the deepest well reaches 900 feet. Use nearby construction reports to estimate a property rather than assuming the median applies exactly.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Evans?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $50 to $70 per foot. At the 49-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,400 to $3,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is about $8,400 to $15,400. A written bid should explain deeper drilling and unsuccessful-hole charges.

faq.q: How much water do Evans wells produce?
faq.a: Among 265 local records reporting pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 15.0 to 900.0 gallons per minute, and 82% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These are recorded results, not a guarantee for a new well, so request the neighboring well reports and a proper pump test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Evans, Colorado?
faq.a: A well permit does not establish drinking-water safety. Local mapping shows 2,478 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with other environmental sites. Test the specific well before relying on it, and review the well location, septic system, and nearby land uses. A qualified laboratory can recommend the right testing panel.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping around Evans?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a simple steady decline. Static water levels were 20 feet below surface in the 1960s, 9 feet in the 2010s, and 13 feet in the 2020s. Because the measurements come from different wells and places, they provide background only. Check the actual well's static level and nearby records.
